tierWindow.goal: Understand what academic research is and how a research project is shaped and structured, before you ever run one.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Understanding, description and recognition with guided application (explain, describe, identify), not designing or critiquing research.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: Well-defined, one idea at a time; the nature of research, the purpose of a proposal and the shape of a project, not the craft of writing each genre.
tierWindow.autonomy: High scaffolding; worked examples; feedback confirms and explains; frequent low-stakes checks. Pitched for a capable beginner.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner is early in their studies and has probably not yet run a research project or written a dissertation. They have met the word 'research' loosely, as looking things up, and need a clear sense of what academic research is and how a project is shaped. No experience of research design, methods or ethics is assumed; teach what research is and the shape of a project from first principles.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, what academic research is: how it differs from simply gathering information. Second, shaping a project: how a research proposal and its questions build the framework for a study. Third, the shape of a research project: the parts that carry it from question to findings. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This short course is about research at university: what academic research actually is, and how a research project is shaped before anyone runs it. By the end you will be able to explain what makes work count as research, describe how a research proposal shapes a project, and recognise the main parts of a research project.

Research is not just looking things up. It is how knowledge is made and tested in every subject, and at some point your degree will ask you to do it, often in a dissertation. Knowing what research is, and how a project is built, makes that moment far less daunting.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain what research is, describe how a proposal shapes a project, recognise the parts of a research project.

practiceConnection.academic: Research underpins your whole degree. Every reading list points to research others have done, every dissertation asks you to do some of your own, and the judgement research demands, asking good questions and weighing evidence, is prized in professional work too. Understanding what research is now gives you a head start when a project lands on your desk.

grounding.note: W-OPEN states the three course outcomes and why they matter (AL-5)

decidedValue.whereNextBody: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced researching courses take you into the research-document genres, such as the literature review and the report, and then into running research with rigour and ethics. Going wider: the same habits underpin Academic Writing, Finding and Using Sources, and Criticality, where you put research to work on real tasks.
decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Research is no longer just a word for looking things up. You can explain what makes work count as research: a focused question answered with evidence towards a defensible conclusion, aiming at a fresh perspective. You can describe how a research proposal and its guiding questions shape a project into something workable. And you can recognise the main parts of a research project, introduction, methodology, results and discussion, and how they carry it from question to findings. Look back at the confidence check to see how far you have moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, research is something you will meet in every part of your degree. Each reading list is built on it, each dissertation asks for some of your own, and the habit of asking a focused question and answering it with evidence is valued well beyond university. The judgement research builds travels into professional work.

courseReferences.title: See pages 145 to 161 of Chapter 9, 'Writing for Assessment', and page 66 of Chapter 5, 'Understanding Assessment', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
